newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG calm, troops hold British mercenary.
newsitem.headline: PNG calm, troops hold British mercenary.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's capital Port Moresby was calm on Saturday after more than 50 African mercenaries were expelled, but army troops were still holding the mercenaries' British commander.
Shopkeepers near the city's main Murray Barracks were sweeping up and replacing window panes smashed by looters and protesters in two days of street violence.
Following a police clampdown on Friday, roadblocks were lifted.
But there were visible signs of continuing tension in the South Pacific nation.
A car reported to belong to the acting army commander installed by Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan lay burnt-out near the barracks entrance. Onlookers said angry soldiers had torched it.
Retired colonel Tim Spicer was being held by army officers opposed to Chan and his plan to bring mercenaries to PNG to end a nine-year guerrilla uprising on copper-rich Bougainville island.

Spicer, a former top U.N. peacekeeper in Bosnia who served in the Falklands and Gulf wars, is chief executive of the British firm Sandline International, which signed a $36 million dollar contract with PNG in January to provide commandos and hardware to crush the Bougainville revolt.

Sandline said in a statement from London that Spicer had been told he could leave with his mercenaries -- veterans from both sides of South Africa's apartheid struggle -- but was kept behind five minutes before their plane left PNG on Friday.

"Sandline found itself enmeshed in a political conflict in which the authority of the legitimate and democratically elected government was challenged by a dissident faction in the PNG Defence Force," the company complained.

Australian radio said Spicer was expected to be handed over to the British High Commission in Port Moresby later on Saturday. Sandline has enlisted British diplomatic help in securing the release of the mercenary commander.

The worst crisis in the 22 years since PNG won independence from Australia began on Monday when army commander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok suddenly turned on Chan, demanding that he quit and terminate the mercenary contract.

Chan promptly sacked him and appointed Colonel Alfred Aikung, an army outsider with a naval background, in his place. Singirok officially accepted his sacking but remained firmly in control of his troops.
Civilians and students angered by poverty and high rates of unemployment backed the army against the government.
On Saturday, soldiers outside Murray Barracks said Aikung was effectively confined to the compound by the troops he has been appointed to lead.

The torched car was covered in angry, ironic death notices. "Graduated from University of Pacific Engineering, majored in corruption, bribes, power-hungry and glory-seeking," said one. "Lest we forget, RIP," read another.
Singirok on Friday renewed his demand for Chan and two senior ministers close to him to quit and set him a deadline of Tuesday, when parliament next sits.
The rebel general wants a caretaker government installed before writs are issued for elections due in June.

The crisis has preoccupied PNG's neighbours, especially Australia. Prime Minister John Howard said on Friday that Australian troops had been put on an increased state of readiness in case the crisis worsened, although he said it was purely a precautionary measure.
Thousands of Australians live and work in PNG.
